blocks.h2: Why Pipes Freeze in Elgin Homes
blocks.intro: Fox Valley winters bring stretches well below freezing. Elgin homes have a few weak spots that freeze first.

items.body: Many homes built before 1940 have little insulation in exterior walls. Kitchen and bathroom pipes on those walls are the first to freeze.
Some older homes have open wall cavities that run from the basement to the attic, letting cold air flow along the pipes.
In newer homes, bathrooms or bedrooms over an attached garage have pipes in a cold floor.
A hose left connected traps water. Older spigots split inside the wall.

blocks.h2: Burst Pipe Questions From Elgin Homeowners

items.q: How do I safely thaw a frozen pipe?
items.preview: Open the faucet and warm the pipe slowly. No open flames.
items.answer: Open the faucet, then warm the pipe slowly with a hair dryer, heating pad or space heater, starting near the faucet. Never use a torch. If you can't reach it, call us.

items.q: How can I keep pipes from freezing in an old house?
items.preview: Keep the heat up, open cabinets on exterior walls and drip faucets in a deep freeze.
items.answer: Keep the heat at 55 degrees or higher, open cabinet doors on exterior walls, let faucets drip on the coldest nights and seal drafts near pipes. We can also insulate or reroute problem lines.

items.q: Why did the leak start after the cold snap ended?
items.preview: The pipe split while frozen and leaked when it thawed.
items.answer: Ice splits the pipe while it's frozen. Water only escapes once it thaws, which is why leaks often appear a day or two later.

items.q: Should I replace my outdoor spigot?
items.preview: If it's old, a freeze-resistant one prevents a common burst.
items.answer: Yes, if it's an older style. A freeze-resistant spigot closes the water off inside the heated part of the wall.
